items.title: What Still Works After It Breaks: Governing AI Systems That Degrade Rather Than Fail
items.body_md:
## The short version

Most operational controls assume failure is an event. Something stops, an alarm sounds, someone responds. AI systems break differently: they carry on running, at full availability, producing fluent output that is increasingly wrong. Nothing sounds. The system is not down, so no incident is raised, and by the time anyone notices, the wrong output has been acted on for weeks.

The governing question is therefore not what can go wrong, but **what still works after it breaks, and would anyone be able to tell?**

---

## 1. Why availability monitoring misses it

A payment system that fails returns errors. An AI system that fails returns answers. The infrastructure is healthy in both the ordinary and the monitored sense: uptime is green, latency is normal, error rates are flat. Every dashboard built for the previous generation of systems reports that nothing is wrong.

What has actually changed sits below that layer. A retrieval index went stale. A model version was updated by a vendor. A data source that fed the system stopped being refreshed. A prompt was edited. In each case the system continues to produce confident, well-formed output, and confidence is the property that makes it dangerous: fluent wrongness is acted upon in a way that an error message never is.

## 2. Degradation is usually silent, and silence is the real problem

There is a difference worth naming between loud waste and quiet waste. A system that fails loudly gets fixed, because it interrupts someone. A system that degrades quietly gets absorbed: users work around it, correct it by hand, or stop relying on it without telling anyone. The organisation loses the value of the system and keeps paying for it, and no incident record exists to explain why.

This has a governance consequence. Controls that trigger on outage will never fire. The register says the system is operating. The review date is months away. Nothing in the machinery is designed to surface the state the system is actually in.

## 3. Design the degraded state deliberately

The alternative is to decide in advance what the system does when it cannot do its job properly, rather than discovering it later. Three principles carry most of the weight.

**Fail to the last known good, not to nothing.** A pipeline stage that cannot reach its source should serve yesterday verified data rather than an empty page. Emptiness looks like a content decision; stale data with a visible date looks like what it is.

**Refuse to publish when output collapses.** If a process that normally produces two thousand records produces four, the correct behaviour is to stop and say so, not to publish four. A threshold against the last known-good run catches the class of failure where the mechanism runs perfectly and the input has vanished.

**Stamp everything with the date it was verified.** A visible as-of date converts an invisible property into a visible one. It costs nothing, it cannot be forgotten by an operator, and it moves the judgement about staleness to the reader, who is often better placed to make it.

## 4. Make the degraded state loud

Every one of those mechanisms should announce itself. A stage that gives up should say so in the log. A source that has stopped being checked should be reported as skipped. A pipeline that falls back to older data should record the fallback rather than pass silently.

The temptation is always to suppress the noise, because a warning that appears every night stops being read. Suppressing the *message* while leaving the *condition* in place is the worst available outcome: it produces a system that looks healthy and is not. If a warning is too frequent to read, the answer is to fix the condition or change the cadence of the check, never to stop reporting it.

## 5. What to ask of any AI system you govern

- When this degrades rather than stops, which signal changes?
- Who sees that signal, and how soon?
- What does it fall back to, and is the fallback visibly marked?
- What would have to be true for us to notice this had been wrong for a month?
- If nobody has raised an incident in a year, is that because it works, or because nothing would tell us?

That last question is the useful one. A control nobody has ever exercised is a control on paper.

## 6. The audit implication

Auditing an AI system on availability, accuracy at a point in time and the existence of a policy will produce a clean report on a system that has been quietly wrong for months. The tests that matter are different in kind: is the deployed configuration the tested configuration, is output reviewed on a stated cadence by a named person, are there thresholds that pause the system, and has any of that machinery ever actually fired.

A control that has never fired is not evidence of a healthy system. It is an untested control, and it should be reported as one.

---

*An independent position paper from theworldofai.org, published by SRJ Consulting & Services LLC. Free to read, free to cite.*

items.title: AI Deployment Readiness Checklist
items.body_md:
## How to use this checklist

Work it before launch, not after. Each item is written so that "no" or "unknown" is a finding you can hand to someone, not a matter of opinion. Anything you cannot answer is itself the answer: an unanswered question at this stage becomes an incident later.

Delete sections that genuinely do not apply. Do not delete them because they are inconvenient — the point of a checklist is that it survives your enthusiasm for the launch.

---

## 1. Do we know what this system is for

- [ ] The decision or task the system performs is written in one sentence, without vendor language.
- [ ] The people affected by its output are named, including anyone who is not the user.
- [ ] The consequence of a wrong output is described in plain terms: who is harmed, how badly, how quickly it would be noticed.
- [ ] Someone is named as accountable for the system by role, not by committee.
- [ ] The decision to build or buy is recorded with the reasoning, so a successor can see why.

## 2. Do we know what goes into it

- [ ] Every data source feeding the system is listed, with its owner.
- [ ] Personal data in those sources is identified, and the lawful basis for using it this way is stated.
- [ ] Data the organisation does not own is separated from data it does, and the licence terms for the former are recorded.
- [ ] Anything a vendor will see, retain, or train on is written down and confirmed with the vendor in writing.
- [ ] The oldest data in the training or retrieval set is dated, and someone has judged whether that age is acceptable for this task.

## 3. Have we tested the thing we are actually shipping

- [ ] Testing used the model, prompt, settings and retrieval sources that will run in production, not an earlier configuration.
- [ ] A test set exists that the system has never seen, and results on it are recorded with a date.
- [ ] Performance is reported by subgroup wherever the system touches people, not only in aggregate — an average conceals exactly the failure that matters.
- [ ] The system was tested with wrong, malicious and empty input, not only with the cases it was designed for.
- [ ] Someone tried to make it produce a harmful output on purpose, and what they found is written down.
- [ ] The failure modes found in testing are listed, with the ones accepted marked as accepted by a named person.

## 4. Can a human intervene

- [ ] The point at which a human can stop or override the system is identified and reachable in the time available.
- [ ] The person expected to override it has the information needed to judge, and the standing to do so without escalation.
- [ ] Automation bias is addressed: the interface shows uncertainty rather than presenting every output with equal confidence.
- [ ] There is a documented way to turn the system off that does not require the vendor.

## 5. Will we know when it goes wrong

- [ ] The system logs its inputs, outputs and the version that produced them, and the logs are retained long enough to investigate.
- [ ] A specific person reviews a sample of output on a stated cadence, and that review is recorded.
- [ ] Degradation is monitored, not just availability: a system producing confident wrong answers at full uptime is the failure that gets missed.
- [ ] Users have a route to report a bad output that does not depend on knowing it is an AI system.
- [ ] Thresholds are set in advance for when the system is paused, and who may pause it.

## 6. Have we told the people who need to know

- [ ] Users are told they are interacting with an AI system, in language they will understand.
- [ ] Where output is used in a decision about someone, that person can find out how to question it.
- [ ] Staff who work alongside the system know what it is for and, more importantly, what it is not for.
- [ ] Any regulatory disclosure that applies to the sector has been checked against this deployment specifically.

## 7. Do we know what happens next

- [ ] A review date is set, with a named owner, before launch rather than after.
- [ ] The conditions that would trigger an early review are written down: a model version change, a data source change, an incident, a regulatory change.
- [ ] Retirement is planned: how the system is switched off, what happens to its data, and who decides.

---

## What a finished checklist is worth

A completed checklist is evidence. Keep the version you actually filled in, with the date and the names, rather than a clean copy — the value to an auditor, a regulator or your own successor lies in the boxes that were not ticked and what was done about them.

items.title: Standing AI Adoption Policy
items.body_md:
## How to use this template

Replace every bracketed field. Delete any clause that does not apply rather than leaving it aspirational: a policy that promises review you do not perform is worse than no policy, because it documents a control you have failed.

This is a template, not legal advice. Have counsel review before adoption if your sector carries specific obligations.

---

## 1. Purpose

[ORGANISATION] uses artificial intelligence tools in the course of its work. This policy states which tools are approved, what may and may not be done with them, and how an employee requests something not on the list. It applies to every employee, contractor, and volunteer, on any device, for any work product.

The policy exists so that the answer to "was this allowed?" is always available before the fact rather than reconstructed after an incident.

## 2. Scope

This policy covers any system that generates, summarises, classifies, translates, or recommends using a machine-learning model, whether purchased, subscribed to, embedded in another product, or free. It covers use in a browser tab as much as use in an integrated system. Personal accounts used for work purposes are in scope; work accounts used for personal purposes are out of scope but not thereby permitted.

## 3. Approved tools

| Tool | Approved for | Not approved for | Data classification permitted | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [TOOL] | [TASKS] | [TASKS] | [PUBLIC / INTERNAL / CONFIDENTIAL] | [NAME] |

Any tool not on this table is unapproved. Unapproved is not the same as forbidden: it means the request path in section 6 has not yet been followed.

## 4. Conditions of use

1. **Data.** Do not enter [CLASSIFICATION] or above into any tool whose row above does not permit it. This includes customer records, personnel matters, unreleased financials, credentials, and anything received under an obligation of confidence.
2. **Verification.** AI output is a draft. The person who submits work is accountable for it, whatever produced it. Verify facts, figures, citations, and quotations against a source before the work leaves your hands.
3. **Disclosure.** Disclose AI assistance where [ORGANISATION] has told a client, regulator, or counterparty that it would, and wherever the recipient would reasonably expect a human author.
4. **Attribution and licence.** Do not represent AI output as the work of a named individual who did not write it. Respect the licence terms of any material you supply as input.
5. **Prohibited uses.** No AI tool may be used to make a final decision about hiring, dismissal, discipline, credit, pricing to an individual, or eligibility for a benefit or service. Those decisions require a named human owner who can explain the reasoning without reference to a model.

## 5. Records

Where an AI tool contributes materially to a decision or a deliverable, record: the tool, the date, the person accountable, and what was verified. [SYSTEM] is the record location. Retain for [PERIOD].

## 6. Requesting a new tool

Send [OWNER] the tool name, vendor, what you want to use it for, what data it would see, and the vendor's terms and privacy page. [OWNER] responds within [N] working days with approved, approved with conditions, or declined and why. Approved tools are added to the table in section 3, which is republished on approval rather than at a review cycle.

## 7. Review

[OWNER] reviews this policy every [PERIOD] and whenever a tool in section 3 materially changes its terms, its data handling, or its model. The review date and the reviewer are recorded on the policy itself.

## 8. Breach

Report suspected breaches to [OWNER]. Reporting your own mistake promptly is treated as compliance with this policy, not as a breach of it. Concealment is the breach.

---

**Version [N] · Adopted [DATE] · Owner [NAME] · Next review [DATE]**

items.title: AI Incident Response Plan
items.body_md:
## How to use this template

This plan sits alongside your existing IT incident process rather than replacing it. The difference it addresses: an IT incident usually announces itself by something stopping, while an AI incident often presents as a system that is running normally and producing confident output that is wrong. Detection therefore cannot rely on availability monitoring.

Replace every bracketed field. This is a template, not legal advice.

---

## 1. What counts as an AI incident

Any of the following, whether or not the system is available:

- Output that is materially wrong, and was acted on or published
- Output that is discriminatory in effect, whatever the intent
- Disclosure of data into or out of a model beyond its approved classification
- A model, prompt, or tool used outside its approved purpose
- Manipulation of a system through its inputs, including prompt injection and poisoned retrieval sources
- An agent taking an action outside the envelope it was granted
- A vendor notifying you of any of the above on their side

Severity is set by consequence, not by cause: [DEFINE SEV1..SEV4 FOR YOUR ORGANISATION].

## 2. Who responds

| Role | Named holder | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Incident lead | [NAME] | Owns the incident end to end, declares and closes it |
| System owner | [NAME] | Knows what the system does and can stop it |
| Data owner | [NAME] | Determines what was exposed and to whom |
| Legal | [NAME] | Regulatory clocks, privilege, notification duties |
| Communications | [NAME] | Anything that leaves the organisation |

Deputies are named for every role. An incident that waits for one person is not a plan.

## 3. Order of response

1. **Detect and record.** Time, reporter, system, what was observed. Start the log at first suspicion, not at confirmation.
2. **Contain.** Stop the system, restrict it, or fall back to the manual process. Containment before diagnosis. A system producing wrong output at scale gets worse while you investigate.
3. **Preserve.** Capture prompts, inputs, outputs, model and version, configuration, and logs before anything is changed. Rotation and retention windows destroy evidence quickly.
4. **Assess scope.** What was produced, over what period, who received it, what decisions followed. Reach for the ceiling first: the earliest plausible start, not the first confirmed one.
5. **Notify.** Run the regulatory clocks in section 4 from the moment of awareness, not the moment of confirmation.
6. **Correct.** Withdraw or reissue affected output, repair the cause, and record what was verified afterwards.
7. **Close and learn.** Written record: what happened, what it cost, what changed. An incident that produces no change to a control is not closed.

## 4. Clocks

| Trigger | Obligation | Clock | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Personal data breach [JURISDICTION] | [OBLIGATION] | [HOURS] | [NAME] |
| Serious incident, EU AI Act, high-risk system | Report to the market surveillance authority | Without undue delay, [SPECIFY YOUR DETERMINATION] | [NAME] |
| Contractual notification | [CUSTOMER TERMS] | [HOURS] | [NAME] |
| Sector-specific | [OBLIGATION] | [HOURS] | [NAME] |

Complete this table from your own obligations before an incident, and confirm each entry with counsel. A clock discovered mid-incident has usually already run.

## 5. What makes AI incidents different

- The system keeps working. Availability monitoring will not find it.
- The output is fluent, so reviewers trust it. Detection often comes from a downstream complaint rather than a control.
- The blast radius is the volume produced, not the duration of an outage.
- Reproduction is unreliable. The same prompt may not produce the same output, which is why preservation comes before diagnosis.
- Vendor dependency is real: you may be unable to investigate a hosted model at all, which is a fact to establish before you need it.

---

**Version [N] · Adopted [DATE] · Owner [NAME] · Next review [DATE]**
items.summary: A response plan for the incident type conventional IT playbooks miss: the system that keeps running, keeps looking confident, and is wrong. Covers what counts as an incident, who responds, and in what order.
items.audience: Anyone who already has an IT incident process and needs the AI-specific additions

items.title: AI Decision Accountability Register
items.body_md:
## How to use this template

Fill one row per decision type, not per decision instance. The register's purpose is to make the accountable human findable before anyone asks, and to make the oversight proportionate to what the decision can do to someone.

Replace every bracketed field. This is a template, not legal advice.

---

## 1. Impact tiers

Classify each decision type by what it does to the person or party affected, not by how sophisticated the system is.

| Tier | Definition | Oversight required |
|---|---|---|
| Critical | Affects a person's livelihood, liberty, health, or legal position | Named human decides. AI output is advisory and recorded as such. Second reviewer for adverse outcomes. |
| High | Material financial or contractual consequence, or hard to reverse | Named human approves before the decision takes effect. Sample review of approvals. |
| Moderate | Consequential but readily reversible | Human review of exceptions and a monitored error rate. |
| Low | Routine, low consequence, easily corrected | Periodic sampling. No per-instance review. |

## 2. The register

| Decision type | System | Tier | Accountable human | Reviewer | Control | Evidence retained | Last reviewed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [e.g. shortlisting applicants] | [TOOL] | Critical | [NAME, ROLE] | [NAME] | [WHAT THE HUMAN ACTUALLY DOES] | [WHAT IS KEPT, WHERE, HOW LONG] | [DATE] |

Rules for completing it honestly:

- **Accountable human** is one named person, not a committee and not a team mailbox.
- **Control** describes what that person does, in verbs. "Reviews the output" is not a control. "Reads the three rejected applications and records a reason for each" is.
- If nobody performs the control described, the row is wrong. Change the control or change the practice, and record which you did.

## 3. The questions this register has to answer

Written so you can test it. Take any row and ask:

1. Who decided? Name.
2. What did the system contribute, and what did the human contribute?
3. What would have happened if the human disagreed with the system, and has that ever happened?
4. What evidence exists that the control was performed, and how long is it kept?
5. When was this last reviewed, and by whom?

If a row cannot answer all five, it is a gap, not a record. Mark it as a gap rather than deleting the row.

## 4. Review cadence

Critical and High rows are reviewed [PERIOD]. Moderate and Low [PERIOD]. Every row is reviewed when its system changes model or vendor, and whenever the decision's consequence changes.

---

**Version [N] · Adopted [DATE] · Owner [NAME] · Next review [DATE]**
items.summary: A register assigning a named human owner to every consequential AI-influenced decision, with oversight scaled to impact. Built so that "the AI decided" is never the answer to a board, regulator, acquirer, or plaintiff.
items.audience: Boards, risk committees, and anyone who will be asked who was accountable

items.title: AI Governance Committee Charter
items.body_md:
## How to use this charter

Replace every bracketed field. Resist the temptation to widen the membership: a committee that cannot reach a decision is worse than no committee, because it converts refusal into delay and gives everyone something to point at.

This is a template, not legal advice.

---

## 1. Purpose

The [ORGANISATION] AI Governance Committee decides which artificial intelligence systems the organisation may use, on what conditions, and when one must stop. It exists so those decisions are made deliberately by people who can be named, rather than accumulating from individual choices nobody reviewed.

## 2. What it decides

The Committee holds decision rights over:

- Approval of any AI system that touches personal data, customer-facing output, employment decisions, or regulated activity.
- The conditions attached to an approval, including monitoring, review dates and limits of use.
- Suspension or withdrawal of a system already in use.
- The organisation-wide AI policy and any exceptions to it.

The Committee does NOT decide procurement price, vendor selection on commercial terms, or technical implementation. Confusing governance with purchasing is the most common way these bodies become slow and irrelevant.

## 3. Membership

| Seat | Held by | Why the seat exists |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chair | [ROLE] | Owns the decision and the record of it |
| Risk or compliance | [ROLE] | Regulatory exposure |
| Technology | [ROLE] | What the system actually does |
| Business owner | Rotating, by system | Consequence of a wrong output lands here |
| Data protection | [ROLE] | Lawful basis and personal data |
| Legal | [ROLE] or on call | Contract and liability |

Quorum is [N], and must include the Chair and one of risk or legal. Members may send a delegate with authority to decide; a delegate who must take it back to their own management does not count toward quorum, because that is how a meeting becomes a status update.

## 4. How it meets

- Scheduled every [FREQUENCY]. A standing meeting that is routinely cancelled should be made less frequent rather than left in the calendar as fiction.
- Any member may call an extraordinary meeting for a suspected incident.
- Papers circulate [N] working days ahead. An item without a paper is not decided, it is noted.

## 5. What a submission must contain

A system is not considered without:

1. What it does, in one sentence, in the words of the person accountable for it.
2. Who is affected, including people who are not users.
3. What happens when it is wrong, and how that would be noticed.
4. Data sources, with personal data and third-party data identified.
5. Test results on data the system has not seen, dated.
6. The human override, and who exercises it.
7. Proposed monitoring and review date.

Incomplete submissions are returned rather than approved conditionally. Conditional approval of an unexamined system is the failure mode this Committee exists to prevent.

## 6. Decisions and the record

Each decision is recorded as approved, approved with conditions, deferred with a stated reason, or refused. The record names the decider, not just the Committee. Minutes state what was decided and on what evidence; a minute that records only attendance and outcome is useless to the person who must revisit the decision in two years.

The Committee maintains a register of every AI system in use, its approval status, its conditions, its owner and its next review date. That register is the real product of this Committee. Everything else is process.

## 7. Escalation

The Committee escalates to [BOARD OR EXECUTIVE BODY] where a decision would breach policy, carries risk beyond its delegated authority, or where members cannot agree. Deadlock is escalated rather than resolved by attrition.

## 8. Review of the Committee itself

Annually, the Committee reviews: how many systems it approved, how many it refused, how many were deployed without coming to it at all, and how many approvals were revisited after an incident. The third number is the honest measure of whether this charter describes reality. If nothing has ever been refused and nothing has ever bypassed the Committee, at least one of those figures is wrong.

---

**Adopted:** [DATE]  ·  **Owner:** [ROLE]  ·  **Next review:** [DATE]

items.title: AI System Audit Workpaper
items.body_md:
## How to use this workpaper

One workpaper per system. Copy it, fill the header, and work the controls in order — later controls assume the earlier ones told you what the system is.

The column that matters is **evidence obtained**, not conclusion. An audit that records conclusions without the artefact behind them cannot be re-performed, and a test that cannot be re-performed did not happen.

Where a control does not apply, write why. Blank means not tested.

---

**System:** [NAME]  ·  **Owner:** [ROLE]  ·  **Period:** [FROM] to [TO]
**Auditor:** [NAME]  ·  **Fieldwork completed:** [DATE]

---

## A. Governance

**A1 — The system is authorised.**
Test: trace the system to a documented approval by whoever holds that authority.
Evidence: approval record naming the decider and the date; conditions attached.
Finding if absent: the organisation is running a system nobody approved. Rate this on consequence, not on the paperwork gap.

**A2 — Accountability is held by a person.**
Test: ask three people who owns the system. Compare answers.
Evidence: role documented; the named holder is aware they hold it.
Finding if absent: ownership by committee, which in practice means ownership by nobody at the moment it fails.

**A3 — The system appears in the AI register.**
Test: reconcile the register against systems actually running, from a source independent of the register itself — expense records, vendor invoices, SSO logs.
Evidence: reconciliation with exceptions listed.
Finding if absent: the register describes what was declared, not what is running. Report the reconciliation gap as the finding, not the missing entry.

## B. Data

**B1 — Data sources are known and lawful.**
Test: list sources; for personal data, obtain the stated lawful basis; for third-party data, obtain the licence.
Evidence: source inventory; DPIA or equivalent where required.
Finding if absent: unable to demonstrate lawful basis, which is a different and more serious finding than an unlawful basis.

**B2 — Data leaving the organisation is controlled.**
Test: determine what the vendor receives, retains and may train on. Obtain the contract clause, not the marketing page.
Evidence: contract extract; configuration screenshot showing retention settings as claimed.
Finding if absent: the control exists in the vendor FAQ and not in the agreement.

## C. Performance

**C1 — The system was tested on data it had not seen.**
Test: obtain evaluation results and confirm the test data was held out.
Evidence: dated results; description of the test set.
Finding if absent: performance is asserted rather than measured.

**C2 — Performance is measured where it matters, not only on average.**
Test: obtain results broken down by the groups the system affects.
Evidence: subgroup results, or a documented reason none are possible.
Finding if absent: aggregate performance conceals the failure that produces the complaint.

**C3 — The tested configuration is the deployed configuration.**
Test: compare model version, prompt, settings and retrieval sources between the evaluation and production.
Evidence: version identifiers from both.
Finding if absent: the evaluation describes a system that is not the one running. This is the most commonly missed control here and the one most likely to invalidate every other result.

## D. Operation

**D1 — A human can intervene, and does.**
Test: identify the override; sample occasions when it was used.
Evidence: log of overrides; interview with the person expected to exercise it.
Finding if absent: an override nobody has ever used is a control on paper. Ask what would have to happen for it to be used, and whether that person would know in time.

**D2 — Output is monitored for quality, not only availability.**
Test: obtain the monitoring definition and a sample review.
Evidence: dated review records; thresholds and who acts on them.
Finding if absent: the system can be wrong at full uptime, indefinitely, and nothing in the monitoring would say so.

**D3 — Incidents are captured and closed.**
Test: trace reported problems from user report to resolution.
Evidence: incident records with dates and outcomes.
Finding if absent: complaints are being handled individually and no pattern is visible to anyone.

---

## Rating findings

Rate on consequence and likelihood, and state both. Avoid rating on how difficult the fix is — remediation effort belongs in the management response, and mixing it into the rating is how a serious finding becomes a medium.

## Management response

Each finding needs an owner by name, an action, and a date. A response reading noted or under review is not a response, and should be recorded as declined so the acceptance of risk is visible to whoever reads this next.

items.title: AI Vendor Scorecard and RFP Questions
items.body_md:
## How to use this

Send the questions. Score the answers, not the demo.

The single most useful discipline here: score a non-answer as a zero rather than leaving it blank. Vendors are practised at answering a different question warmly, and a blank cell quietly becomes a pass by the time the scorecard reaches a decision meeting.

Replace bracketed fields. Weightings are a starting point; change them to match what would actually hurt you.

---

## Scorecard

| Area | Weight | Score 0-5 | Weighted |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fitness for the stated task | 20% | | |
| Data handling and retention | 20% | | |
| Security posture | 15% | | |
| Transparency about the model | 10% | | |
| Evaluation evidence | 10% | | |
| Human oversight and control | 10% | | |
| Contractual protection | 10% | | |
| Exit and portability | 5% | | |

**Scoring:** 5 evidenced with documents we can keep · 4 evidenced in writing · 3 stated credibly, unevidenced · 2 partial or hedged · 1 deflected · 0 not answered, or answered with a different question.

Any area scoring 0 or 1 goes to the decision meeting as a named risk with an owner. A total score means little; the pattern of zeros means a great deal.

---

## The questions

### Fitness for the task

1. What exactly does the product do, described without the words powerful, seamless or intelligent?
2. On what task was it measured, and what did it score?
3. What does it do badly? A vendor who cannot answer this has not tested it or will not tell you.
4. Which of our use cases have you seen fail elsewhere?
5. What happens to output quality on inputs unlike your training data?

### Data handling

6. What data do you retain, for how long, and where?
7. Is our data used to train or improve your models, by default or ever? Point to the clause.
8. Who at your organisation can see our data, and under what process?
9. Which subprocessors touch our data, and where are they?
10. Can we require deletion, and what is the proven timescale?
11. What happens to our data on termination, and in what format do we get it back?
12. Do you support regional data residency, and is it contractual or best-effort?

### Security

13. When was your last third-party penetration test, and may we see the summary?
14. What certifications do you hold, and what is their scope? Scope matters more than the badge.
15. How do you handle prompt injection against our data through your product?
16. How is our tenant isolated from other customers?
17. What is your breach notification commitment in hours, in the contract?
18. How do you authenticate and log administrative access to systems holding our data?

### Transparency about the model

19. Which model or models serve our requests today?
20. Will you notify us before changing the underlying model, and how far ahead?
21. Is the model yours, or licensed from a third party? If licensed, what obligations pass to us?
22. Where are you in the EU AI Act classification for our intended use, and what does that make us?

### Evaluation evidence

23. Show us evaluation results on data the model had not seen.
24. Do you report performance by subgroup, or only in aggregate?
25. How do you test for the failure that matters to us specifically?
26. What monitoring will tell us the system has degraded after we deploy it?

### Human oversight

27. Where can a person intervene, and what does that person see?
28. Does the interface communicate uncertainty, or present every output identically?
29. Can we disable a feature without leaving the product?
30. What audit log do we get, and can we export it?

### Contract

31. Who is liable when the output is wrong and we relied on it?
32. What indemnity do you offer for intellectual property claims arising from output?
33. Are your service levels about availability only, or about quality?
34. What are the terms for price change at renewal?
35. May we audit, or receive the report of someone who did?

### Exit

36. How do we get our data out, in what format, and how long does it take?
37. What of our configuration and history is portable, and what is lost?
38. What happens if you are acquired, or discontinue the product?
39. What is the shortest exit we could execute if we had to leave in ninety days?
40. Name a customer who left. What did that look like?

---

## Reading the answers

Question 3 and question 40 do most of the work. A vendor who can describe their own weaknesses and an unhappy departure is usually telling the truth elsewhere. A vendor who cannot is not necessarily lying, but you have no way to know, and that in itself is the finding.
items.summary: A weighted scorecard and forty questions to put to an AI vendor, written so that a vague answer scores badly instead of passing.
items.audience: Anyone evaluating an AI product, or writing the AI section of an RFP
items.based_on: ISO/IEC 42001:2023, the EU AI Act transparency obligations, and NIST AI RMF Map
